1.q: הָב֣וּ לַֽ֭⁠יהוָה בְּנֵ֣י אֵלִ֑ים הָב֥וּ לַ֝⁠יהוָ֗ה כָּב֥וֹד וָ⁠עֹֽז
1.note: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Ascribe these things to Yahweh, sons of God, ascribe to Yahweh glory and strength]

David assumes that readers will know that **sons of God** refers to angels or heavenly beings. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you angels]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory** and **strength**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [acknowledge that Yahweh is glorious and strong] or [praise Yahweh because he is glorious and strong]

2.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Declare that Yahweh is glorious because of his name] or [Praise Yahweh for how glorious his name is]

David is using this possessive form **the glory of his name** to mean the glory that his name deserves. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the glory his name deserves]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the glory due to Yahweh] or [the glory Yahweh’s reputation deserves]

Here, **bow down** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and worship to Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [bow down in worship to Yahweh]

The phrase **adornment of holiness** refers to the garments the Levitical priests wore while serving in Yahweh’s tabernacle. David is using the possessive form to describe **adornment** that is characterized by **holiness** because of the purpose for which it was made. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this purpose, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in holy adornment] or [in adornment that is holy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in holy clothing]

3.note: See the Psalm 29 Introduction for more information regarding the historical and religious background of verses 3–10.

The phrase **The voice of Yahweh** could: (1) refer to the actual voice of Yahweh or (2) this phrase could mean “The thunder of Yahweh” since this phrase sometimes had that meaning in Hebrew. Alternate translation: [The thunder of Yahweh is over the waters]
By **the waters**, David means the sea and here he probably specifically means the Mediterranean Sea. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use plain language as in the UST.

3.q: ק֥וֹל יְהוָ֗ה עַל־הַ֫⁠מָּ֥יִם & יְ֝הוָ֗ה עַל־מַ֥יִם רַבִּֽים
3.note: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The voice of Yahweh is heard over the waters … Yahweh’s voice is heard over many waters]
Here the word the ULT translates as **over**, both times it occurs in this verse, could mean: (1) **over**, as in the ULT, or (2) “against.” Alternate translation: [is against … is against]

The phrase **the God of glory thunders** could mean: (1) that Yahweh’s powerful voice sounds like thunder. Alternate translation: [the glorious God speaks with a voice like thunder] or [the God of glory speaks powerfully], or (2) that Yahweh sends thunder. Alternate translation: [the God of glory sends thunder]

David is using the possessive form to describe **the God** who is characterized by **glory**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the glorious God]

4.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **power** and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [The voice of Yahweh is powerful; the voice of Yahweh is majestic]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. David is emphasizing the awesome nature of Yahweh’s voice by using both **power** and **majesty** to describe it. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [The voice of Yahweh is very powerful]

5.note: Here, **voice** represents the sound of Yahweh’s voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

5.q: ק֣וֹל יְ֭הוָה שֹׁבֵ֣ר אֲרָזִ֑ים וַ⁠יְשַׁבֵּ֥ר יְ֝הוָ֗ה אֶת־אַרְזֵ֥י הַ⁠לְּבָנֽוֹן
5.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [The voice of Yahweh is breaking cedars, yes, breaking the cedars of Lebanon]

6.q: וַ⁠יַּרְקִידֵ֥⁠ם כְּמוֹ־עֵ֑גֶל לְבָנ֥וֹן וְ֝⁠שִׂרְיֹ֗ן כְּמ֣וֹ בֶן־רְאֵמִֽים
6.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [And he makes Lebanon and Sirion skip like calves, like young wild oxen]

6.q: וַ⁠יַּרְקִידֵ֥⁠ם כְּמוֹ־עֵ֑גֶל לְבָנ֥וֹן וְ֝⁠שִׂרְיֹ֗ן כְּמ֣וֹ בֶן־רְאֵמִֽים
6.note: David is comparing how Lebanon and Sirion shake to how young animals jump around. The point of this comparison is that just as **a calf** and **a son of wild oxen** skip and jump with energetic movement, so do these mountains shake when God’s voice thunders. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And he makes Lebanon shake with energetic movement like a calf, and Sirion like a son of wild oxen]
The word **Sirion** is the name of a mountain. It is another name for Mount Hermon. If it would help your readers, you could use that name instead as in the UST.

David assumes that readers will know that **a son of wild oxen** means a young wild ox. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a young wild ox]

7.note: The phrase **The voice of Yahweh** could: (1) refer to the actual voice of Yahweh, or (2) could mean “The thunder of Yahweh” since this phrase sometimes has that meaning in Hebrew. Alternate translation: [The thunder of Yahweh is hewing out with flames of fire] See how you translated the phrase **The voice of Yahweh** in verse 3.

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [is hewing out stone] or [is hewing out rock]

By **flames of fire**, David means lightning. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with lightning] or [with flashes of lightning]

8.note: Here, **voice** represents the sound of Yahweh’s voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly as in the UST.
The word **Kadesh** is the name of a place.

9.note: Here, **voice** represents the sound of Yahweh’s voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

Here David is speaking of Yahweh’s tabernacle in Jerusalem as if it were a **temple**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in his tabernacle]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [How glorious Yahweh is]

10.q: יְ֭הוָה לַ⁠מַּבּ֣וּל יָשָׁ֑ב וַ⁠יֵּ֥שֶׁב יְ֝הוָ֗ה מֶ֣לֶךְ לְ⁠עוֹלָֽם
10.note: Here both times the word **sits** is used, it represents “ruling” as king since at that time kings sat on a throne from which they ruled, made decisions, and gave commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.
David assumes that readers will know that **sits** means “rules as king.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh sits enthroned … as]

The phrase **the flood** could refer to: (1) the water that is above the sky as in the UST, or (2) the great flood recorded in Genesis chapters 6–9 that God sent during the time of Noah. Alternate translation: [over the flood that covered the earth] or [over the Flood]

11.q: יְֽהוָ֗ה עֹ֭ז לְ⁠עַמּ֣⁠וֹ יִתֵּ֑ן יְהוָ֓ה ׀ יְבָרֵ֖ךְ אֶת־עַמּ֣⁠וֹ בַ⁠שָּׁלֽוֹם
11.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **peace**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will make his people strong; Yahweh will bless his people so that they live peacefully]
